searchDocs.title: Software of interest
searchDocs.content: Software of interest To install this software use the package manager, apt, dnf or pacman. firefox: browser.emacs: text editor.vim: terminal text editor.alacritty: terminal.git: version control.python-pip: python package manager.Developement tools: install compilers, make, etc ... Debian: build-essential.Fedora: Development Tools, C Development Tools and Libraries. (dnf group list)Arch: base-devel. gfortran: fortran compiler.cmake: build tool.meson: build tool.unzip7zipxorg-xrandr: manage displaysarandr: xrandr frontend.man-db: install manpages.xdg-user-dirs: install default user dirs of the system.networkmanagernetwork-manager-applet: applet to use network manager.blueman: bluetooth.bluez: bluetooth.bluez-utils: bluetooth. (only on Arch)brightnessctl : for laptop.pavucontrol: volume control.thunar: file manager.smbclient: samba client.cifs-utils: needed for open samba shares on thunar.gvfs: virtual filesystem support (needed for mounting via Thunar).gvfs-smb: Support for samba share.gvfs-backends: Needed for samba share. (only on Debian)xclip: clipboard.bat: cat but beautiful.fzf: fuzzy finder.btop: top but beautiful.feh: wallpaper.picom: lightweight X11 compositor (graphic effects, vsync).flameshot: screenshots.wgettexlive: latex.exa: display icons when doing ls.os-prober: needed to configure grub and detect other systems if not detected by default.grub: needed to configure grub and detect other systems if not detected by default.

searchDocs.title: Alacritty
searchDocs.content: Alacritty To install Alacritty use the following commands, depending on your system: Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get install alacritty Fedora: sudo dnf install alacritty Arch: sudo pacman -S alacritty In the home directory, create a file called .alacritty.toml if it does not exist yet. Write the following configuration and change things to match your preferences: [font] size = 12.0 [font.bold] family = "DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font" style = "Bold" [font.bold_italic] family = "DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font" style = "Bold Italic" [font.italic] family = "DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font" style = "Italic" [font.normal] family = "DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font" style = "Regular" [font.offset] x = 1 y = 5 [selection] save_to_clipboard = true [terminal.shell] program = "/bin/bash" [window] decorations = "full" decorations_theme_variant = "Dark" dynamic_padding = true opacity = 1.0 [window.padding] x = 5 y = 5 [terminal]

searchDocs.title: Install Oh-my-bash
searchDocs.content: Install Oh-my-bash Execute the wget or curl installation command found in their GitHub page. At the moment of writing this documentation is the one below: bash -c "$(wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmybash/oh-my-bash/master/tools/install.sh -O -)" In order to see the themes correctly, you need to have some NerdFonts installed. Bashrc Apply some modifications to the .bashrc file found in the home directory. Change OSH_THEME to the theme of your preference, in this case rr: OSH_THEME="rr" Configure eza. This step is not necessary and not related to Oh-my-bash. Install eza: Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get install eza Fedora sudo dnf install eza Arch sudo pacman -S eza Create an alias for eza: alias ls='eza -l --icons --group-directories-first -h --total-size'

searchDocs.title: Install Arch Linux​
searchDocs.content: The full guide of how to install Arch Linux can be found in Arch wiki.

searchDocs.title: Keymap​
searchDocs.content: loadkeys es

searchDocs.title: Internet​
searchDocs.content: Ethernet​  Nothing to do.  Wifi​  The full guide on how to use iwclt can be found in this address. In my case:  iwctl   [iwd] # device list   This will show a list with all the wireless devices. Let's use the device name wlan0.  [iwd] # station wlan0 scan [iwd] # station wlan0 get-networks   This will scan and show all the SSID of the wireless networks around. Let's say the SSID is WIRELESS-CONN-1.  [iwd] # station wlan0 connect WIRELESS-CONN-1   Write the password and check if the connection is established, doing ping to Google:  ping www.google.es

searchDocs.title: Launch the assistant​
searchDocs.content: archinstall   Follow the instructions and choose i3wm installation. Select PulseAudio, and NetworkManager. At this stage, it is mandatory to install networkmanager and network-manager-applet. Also very useful to install the web browser.

searchDocs.title: TODO things after installation​
searchDocs.content: Update the system:  sudo pacman -Syu   If programs are not installed, install them by using the command:  sudo pacman -S name-of-the-program   Example of a base installation:  sudo pacman -S emacs vim alacritty git python-pip base-devel gcc-fortran cmake meson unzip 7zip arandr man-db xdg-user-dirs blueman bluez bluez-utils pavucontrol thunar smbclient cifs-utils gvfs gvfs-smb xclip bat fzf btop feh exa wget xorg-xrandr flameshot picom   Enable bluetooth:  sudo systemctl enable --now bluetooth   Create user directories:  xdg-user-dirs-update   Reboot:  reboot

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: Create the user-installed fonts directory:  mkdir -p ~/.local/share/fonts   Download and extract the fonts inside the folder created by the above command.

searchDocs.title: Linux usefull bash commands
searchDocs.content: Linux usefull bash commands Command	Descriptionaddgroup	Adds a group to the system. apropos	Searches through man pages' descriptions for instances of a given keyword. bg	Puts a process into background. cat	Concatenate and print files. cd	Changes the directory. clear	Clears the terminal. column	Command-line based utility that formats its input into multiple columns. cp	Copy files or directories. curl	Command-line utility to transfer data from or to a server. cut	Removes sections from each line of files. delgroup	Removes a group from the system. dpkg	Install, remove and configure Debian-based packages. du	Shows how much disk space is used by files and directories. env	Prints environment or sets and executes a command. fg	Puts a process into the foreground. find	Searches for files in a directory hierarchy. grep	Searches for specific results that contain given patterns. head	Prints the first ten lines of STDOUT or a file. hostname	Sets or prints the name of the current host system. id	Returns users identity. ip	Ip is a utility to show or manipulate routing, network devices, interfaces, and tunnels. jobs	Lists all processes that are running in the background. journalctl	Query the systemd journal. kill	Sends a signal to a process. less	An alternative to more with more features. ls	Lists directory contents. lsblk	Lists block devices. lsusb	Lists USB devices. lsof	Lists opened files. lspci	Lists PCI devices. man	Opens man pages for the specified tool. mkdir	Creates a directory. more	Pager that is used to read STDOUT or files. mv	Move or rename files or directories. netstat	Shows network status. passwd	Changes user password. ps	Shows process status. pwd	Returns working directory name. rename	Renames files. rm	Removes files or directories. rmdir	Removes empty directories. ss	Another utility to investigate sockets. sort	Sorts the contents of STDOUT or a file. sudo	Execute command as a different user. su	The su utility requests appropriate user credentials via PAM and switches to that user ID (the default user is the superuser). A shell is then executed. systemctl	Command-line based service and systemd control manager. tail	Prints the last ten lines of STDOUT or a file. touch	Creates an empty file. tr	Replaces certain characters. tree	Lists the contents of a directory recursively. uname	Prints operating system name. usermod	Modifies a user account. useradd	Creates a new user or update default new user information. userdel	Deletes a user account and related files. which	Returns the path to a file or link. wc	Prints newline, word, and byte counts for a given input. whoami	Displays current username. who	Displays who is logged in. wget	An alternative to curl that downloads files from FTP or HTTP(s) server. xml	Marks up or manipulates XML content.

searchDocs.content: To install X11 execute the following command:  sudo apt install xorg

searchDocs.title: lightdm​

searchDocs.title: Gtk 3.0: Dark theme​
searchDocs.content: Create folder ~/.config/gtk-3.0:  mkdir ~/.config/gtk-3.0   Move to gtk-3.0 folder and create two files, bookmarks and settings.ini  touch bookmarks touch settings.ini   Leave bookmarks empty and write the following in settings.ini:  [Settings] gtk-application-prefer-dark-theme=true

searchDocs.title: lxappearance​
searchDocs.content: Frontend to configure system themes. Install using the following command:  Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt install lxappearance   Fedora:  sudo dnf install lxappearance   Arch:  sudo pacman -S lxappearance

searchDocs.title: Wallpapers​
searchDocs.content: Create the folder ~/.config/wallpapers and copy the wallpapers there:  mkdir ~/.config/wallpapers   If it is not installed, install feh.  Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt-get install feh   Fedora:  sudo dnf install feh   Arch:  sudo pacman -S feh   To set the the wallpaper is necessary to modify the i3wm configuration file and add the following line:  exec feh --bg-fill ~/.config/wallpapers/name-wallpaper.jpg

searchDocs.title: Picom​
searchDocs.content: Create the file to hold the configuration file for Picom:  mkdir .config/picom touch .config/picom/picom.conf   Edit picom.conf file and write the following:  backend = "glx"; # Use OpenGL to improve performance vsync = true; # This avoids tearing. glx-no-stencil = true; glx-no-rebind-pixmap = true; use-damage = true; # Other useful options refresh-rate = 0; # 0 = autodetect vsync-use-glfinish = false; unredir-if-possible = false; # This is important to vsync work correctly. # Transparencies (optional) shadow = false; fading = false;

searchDocs.title: Install Debian​
searchDocs.content: The full guide of how to install Debian can be found in Debian site. The installation of Debian is quite stragith forward. The most interesting part is on the selection of the desktop enviroment. To minimal installation without any desktop enviroment, unselect the default desktop enviroment. Usefull for servers or for desktop enviroments or window managers not present in the installation.

searchDocs.title: First boot​
searchDocs.content: Update and upgrade the system.  sudo apt update -y && sudo apt upgrade -y

searchDocs.title: Configure Emacs​
searchDocs.content: A basic Emacs configuration starts by editing the init.el file foun in the ~/.emacs.d/ directory. An example of a simple Emacs configuration can be found here. Just copy the init.el and the emacs.custom.el file to ~/.emacs.d folder.  Note: To build vterm it is necessary to have installed C/C++ compilers, make and Cmake. It is also possible to use the configuration without vterm by commenting the line at respect in the init.el config file.

searchDocs.title: Copilot​
searchDocs.content: If my configuration is used and the copilot section is not commentted, then it is necessary to install the following. (Requirements: to have installed npm)  To use Copilot, do the following (requirement: install npm):  Download the Emacs plugin:  git clone https://github.com/copilot-emacs/copilot.el ~/.emacs.d/copilot   Download and install copilot cli.  npm -g --prefix ~/.emacs.d/.cache/copilot install @github/copilot-language-server   Open emacs and run:  M-x copilot-install-server M-x copilot-login

searchDocs.title: Language Server Protocol (LSP)​
searchDocs.content: To use LSP within Emacs is necessary to install the LSP servers for C/C++, Python and Fortran.

searchDocs.title: C/C++​
searchDocs.content: Install clangd.  Debian/Ubuntu:  sudo apt-get install clangd   Fedora:  sudo dnf install clang-tools-extra   Arch:  sudo pacman -S clang

searchDocs.title: Python​
searchDocs.content: Install pyright using pip:  pip install pyright   To install pyright system wide in some Linux distributions, it is necessary to run the following command:  pip install pyright --break-system-packages

searchDocs.title: Fortran​
searchDocs.content: Install fortls using pip:  pip install fortls   Similar to pyright, in some systems it asks to break system packages.  pip install fortls --break-system-packages

searchDocs.title: Raspberry Pi OS​
searchDocs.content: The fastest way is to download the Raspberry Pi Imager, and follow the instructions to download the Lite version of the Raspberry Pi OS. This is the version without any Desktop Enviroment installed. The system has to be installed on a SD Card. Once the process is finished, insert the SD Card into the slot on the Raspberry Pi, so the system can be loaded for the first time. After the first boot, update and upgrade the system.  sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get upgrade -y

searchDocs.title: Enable SSH​
searchDocs.content: Enable SSH is usefull to configure the Raspberry Pi remotely. The SSH connection is enable through the Raspberry Pi configuration.  sudo raspi-config   Then select the third option, Interface Options, and I1 SSH to enable it. Once it is enable, it is possible to connect from other computer in the same network by writting the following command:  ssh <pi-username>@<ip-raspberry>   Example:  Pi username: NasPiIp raspberry: 192.168.1.23  ssh NasPi@192.168.1.23   Note: after introducing the credentials it will ask for a password.

searchDocs.title: Setting up an static IP​
searchDocs.content: The static IP is set up through the Network Manager application. The first step is to identify the connection and save the name.  nmcli connection show   This will show something like this.  NAME UUID TYPE DEVICE Wired connection 1 4b3b674a-d346-5cfa-3b30-df70e6db4b81 ethernet eth0   Then it's time to modify the connection.  nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \ ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.78/24 \ ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \ ipv4.method manual   After this command the IP of the Raspberry Pi is set to 192.168.1.78, and the change is persistent.

searchDocs.title: RAID 1 storage​
searchDocs.content: There are different types of RAID storages. The RAID 1 storage consists on create a mirror of a set of data on two or more disks. For the purpose of a home NAS, using two disks and RAID 1 configuration is enough. But this is something to evaluate in each case.  To create the RAID 1 virtual disk, the program mdadm has to be installed as follow.  sudo apt install mdadm   The next step consists on listing the disks.  lsblk   Here there is an example of the output.  NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS loop0 7:0 0 2G 0 loop sda 8:0 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sda1 8:1 0 3.6T 0 part sdc 8:32 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sdc1 8:33 0 3.6T 0 part zram0 253:0 0 2G 0 disk [SWAP] nvme0n1 259:0 0 238.5G 0 disk ├─nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 512M 0 part /boot/firmware └─nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 238G 0 part /   So the two disk, 3.6TB in this case, are sda and sdc. So to create the device associated to the RAID, the following command is used:  sudo mdadm --create /dev/md0 \ --level=1 \ --raid-devices=2 \ /dev/sda /dev/sdc   If the disks are listed again, the device md0 will appear.  NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS loop0 7:0 0 2G 0 loop sda 8:0 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sda1 8:1 0 3.6T 0 part └─md0 9:0 0 3.6T 0 raid1 /mnt/raid1 sdc 8:32 0 3.6T 0 disk └─sdc1 8:33 0 3.6T 0 part zram0 253:0 0 2G 0 disk [SWAP] nvme0n1 259:0 0 238.5G 0 disk ├─nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 512M 0 part /boot/firmware └─nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 238G 0 part /   Then format the file sytem to EXT4.  sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/md0   Finally, create a mount point for the unit.  sudo mkdir /mnt/raid1 sudo mount /dev/md0 /mnt/raid1   To make the mount point permanent, find the UUID of the device md0. Execute the following command and save the UUID returned value.  sudo blkid /dev/md0   Then edit the file /etc/fstab and add the following line.  proc /proc proc defaults 0 0 ... UUID=4b3b674a-d346-5cfa-2f40-ef70e6db4c94 /mnt/raid1 ext4 defaults,nofail 0 0 ...   Finally save the RAID configuration to mdadm.conf.  sudo mdadm --detail --scan | sudo tee -a /etc/mdadm/mdadm.conf   The last step is to update initramfs and reboot the system.  sudo update-initramfs -u reboot

searchDocs.title: Configure SMB​
searchDocs.content: Install Samba:  sudo apt update sudo apt install samba samba-common-bin

searchDocs.title: Create system users​
searchDocs.content: To create Samba users, those need to exist as a system users too. Those users do not need to have home and the login can be disabled.  sudo adduser --no-create-home --disabled-login user1 sudo adduser --no-create-home --disabled-login user2   So the creation and activation of a Samba user linked to the system user, can be done by running the following command.  sudo smbpasswd -a userX sudo smbpasswd -e userX   The edit the file /etc/samba/smb.conf and add the users like that:  [user1] path = /mnt/raid1 browseable = yes read only = no valid users = user1 [user2] path = /mnt/raid1 browseable = yes read only = no valid users = user2

searchDocs.title: Force to use SMB3 protocol​
searchDocs.content: In the previous same file, under the [global] section add the following lines.  [global] ... ## Force samba SMB3 protocol ### client min protocol = SMB3 server min protocol = SMB3 ...

searchDocs.title: Reboot the Samba service​
searchDocs.content: sudo systemctl restart smbd

searchDocs.title: Reboot the system​
searchDocs.content: sudo reboot

searchDocs.title: Installation​
searchDocs.content: i3wm can be selected during the installation in Arch Linux, and Fedora has it's own i3 spin. So only the case of Debian is shown here. Before the installation of the i3wm it is necessary to install xorg and any display manager. The command to install xorg, ssdm and i3wm is:  sudo apt install xorg sddm i3

searchDocs.title: i3wm configuration​
searchDocs.content: The main files are in ~/.config/i3/config and ~/.config/i3status/config. Below there is a configuration example:

searchDocs.title: i3wm config file​
searchDocs.content: Open the file ~/.config/i3/config delete its contents and paste the following:  # This file has been auto-generated by i3-config-wizard(1). # It will not be overwritten, so edit it as you like. # # Should you change your keyboard layout some time, delete # this file and re-run i3-config-wizard(1). # # i3 config file (v4) # # Please see https://i3wm.org/docs/userguide.html for a complete reference! set $mod Mod4 # Font for window titles. Will also be used by the bar unless a different font # is used in the bar {} block below. font pango:DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font 12 # This font is widely installed, provides lots of unicode glyphs, right-to-left # text rendering and scalability on retina/hidpi displays (thanks to pango). #font pango:DejaVu Sans Mono 8 # Start XDG autostart .desktop files using dex. See also # https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/XDG_Autostart exec --no-startup-id dex --autostart --environment i3 # The combination of xss-lock, nm-applet and pactl is a popular choice, so # they are included here as an example. Modify as you see fit. # xss-lock grabs a logind suspend inhibit lock and will use i3lock to lock the # screen before suspend. Use loginctl lock-session to lock your screen. exec --no-startup-id xss-lock --transfer-sleep-lock -- i3lock -c 000000 --nofork bindsym $mod+Mod1+l exec i3lock -c 000000 # NetworkManager is the most popular way to manage wireless networks on Linux, # and nm-applet is a desktop environment-independent system tray GUI for it. exec --no-startup-id nm-applet # Blueman for bluetooth exec --no-startup-id blueman-applet # Set resolution at start #exec xrandr --output HDMI-0 --primary --mode 1920x1080 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-0 --mode 2560x1440 --rate 144 - #bindsym $mod+o exec xrandr --output eDP-1 --primary --mode 1920x1200 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-1-0 --off --output DP-1-1 --off --output DP-1-2 --off --output DP-1-3 --off --output HDMI-1-0 --off --output DP-1-4 --off #bindsym $mod+Shift+o exec xrandr --output eDP-1 --primary --mode 1920x1200 --pos 0x0 --rotate normal --output DP-1-0 --off --output DP-1-1 --off --output DP-1-2 --off --output DP-1-3 --off --output HDMI-1-0 --mode 1920x1080 --pos 2560x204 --rotate normal --output DP-1-4 --off # Wallpaper exec feh --bg-scale ~/.config/wallpapers/lake-mountains-rocks-sunrise-daylight-scenery-illustration-6016x6016-3773.jpg # Picom: copositor exec --no-startup-id picom --config ~/.config/picom/picom.conf # Use pactl to adjust volume in PulseAudio. set $refresh_i3status killall -SIGUSR1 i3status bindsym XF86AudioRaiseVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ +5% && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioLowerVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ -5% && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-mute @DEFAULT_SINK@ toggle && $refresh_i3status bindsym XF86AudioMicMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-source-mute @DEFAULT_SOURCE@ toggle && $refresh_i3status # Brightness #bindsym XF86MonBrightnessUp exec brightnessctl -d intel_backlight s +5% > /dev/null && notify-send Brightness $(($(brightnessctl get) * 10 / 937 * 10))% -h string:x-canonical-private-synchronous:brightness_percentage --app-name System #bindsym XF86MonBrightnessDown exec brightnessctl -d intel_backlight s 5%- > /dev/null && notify-send Brightness $(($(brightnessctl get) * 10 / 937 * 10))% -h string:x-canonical-private-synchronous:brightness_percentage --app-name System # Use Mouse+$mod to drag floating windows to their wanted position floating_modifier $mod # move tiling windows via drag & drop by left-clicking into the title bar, # or left-clicking anywhere into the window while holding the floating modifier. tiling_drag modifier titlebar # start a terminal #bindsym $mod+Return exec i3-sensible-terminal bindsym $mod+Return exec alacritty # kill focused window bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill # start dmenu (a program launcher) bindsym $mod+d exec --no-startup-id dmenu_run -fn 'DaddyTimeMono Nerd Font:regular:pixelsize=20' # A more modern dmenu replacement is rofi: # bindcode $mod+40 exec "rofi -modi drun,run -show drun" # There also is i3-dmenu-desktop which only displays applications shipping a # .desktop file. It is a wrapper around dmenu, so you need that installed. # bindcode $mod+40 exec --no-startup-id i3-dmenu-desktop # change focus bindsym $mod+j focus left bindsym $mod+k focus down bindsym $mod+l focus up bindsym $mod+ntilde focus right # alternatively, you can use the cursor keys: bindsym $mod+Left focus left bindsym $mod+Down focus down bindsym $mod+Up focus up bindsym $mod+Right focus right # move focused window bindsym $mod+Shift+j move left bindsym $mod+Shift+k move down bindsym $mod+Shift+l move up bindsym $mod+Shift+ntilde move right # alternatively, you can use the cursor keys: bindsym $mod+Shift+Left move left bindsym $mod+Shift+Down move down bindsym $mod+Shift+Up move up bindsym $mod+Shift+Right move right # split in horizontal orientation bindsym $mod+h split h # switch to workspace bindsym $mod+1 workspace number $ws1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace number $ws2 bindsym $mod+3 workspace number $ws3 bindsym $mod+4 workspace number $ws4 bindsym $mod+5 workspace number $ws5 bindsym $mod+6 workspace number $ws6 bindsym $mod+7 workspace number $ws7 bindsym $mod+8 workspace number $ws8 bindsym $mod+9 workspace number $ws9 bindsym $mod+0 workspace number $ws10 # move focused container to workspace bindsym $mod+Shift+1 move container to workspace number $ws1 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace number $ws2 bindsym $mod+Shift+3 move container to workspace number $ws3 bindsym $mod+Shift+4 move container to workspace number $ws4 bindsym $mod+Shift+5 move container to workspace number $ws5 bindsym $mod+Shift+6 move container to workspace number $ws6 bindsym $mod+Shift+7 move container to workspace number $ws7 bindsym $mod+Shift+8 move container to workspace number $ws8 bindsym $mod+Shift+9 move container to workspace number $ws9 bindsym $mod+Shift+0 move container to workspace number $ws10 # reload the configuration file bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload # restart i3 inplace (preserves your layout/session, can be used to upgrade i3) bindsym $mod+Shift+r restart # exit i3 (logs you out of your X session) bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'You pressed the exit shortcut. Do you really want to exit i3? This will end your X session.' -B 'Yes, exit i3' 'i3-msg exit'" # resize window (you can also use the mouse for that) mode "resize" { # These bindings trigger as soon as you enter the resize mode # Pressing left will shrink the window’s width. # Pressing right will grow the window’s width. # Pressing up will shrink the window’s height. # Pressing down will grow the window’s height. bindsym j resize shrink width 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym k resize grow height 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym l resize shrink height 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym ntilde resize grow width 10 px or 10 ppt # same bindings, but for the arrow keys bindsym Left resize shrink width 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym Down resize grow height 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym Up resize shrink height 10 px or 10 ppt bindsym Right resize grow width 10 px or 10 ppt # back to normal: Enter or Escape or $mod+r bindsym Return mode "default" bindsym Escape mode "default" bindsym $mod+r mode "default" } bindsym $mod+r mode "resize" bindsym $mod+b exec chromium bindsym $mod+t exec thunar bindsym $mod+c exec emacs # Start i3bar to display a workspace bar (plus the system information i3status # finds out, if available) bar { status_command i3status }

searchDocs.content: Create the folder i3status if it does not exist, and then create a file named config inside:  mkdir ~/.config/i3status touch ~/.config/i3status/config   Open the file config, paste the content below. The i3status config file below is just an example. It might require some modificatons to work.  general { output_format = "i3bar" colors = true color_good = "#a3be8c" color_degraded = "#ebcb8b" color_bad = "#bf616a" interval = 30 separator = "|" } order += "cpu_usage" order += "disk /" order += "disk /home" order += "memory" order += "ethernet enp12s0" order += "wireless wlan0" order += "battery all" order += "volume master" order += "tztime madrid" cpu_usage { format = %usage degraded_threshold = 90 max_threshold = 95 } wireless wlan0 { format_up = "W: (%quality at %essid, %bitrate) %ip" format_down = "W: down" } ethernet enp12s0 { format_up = "E: %ip (%speed)" format_down = "E: down" } battery all { format = "%status %percentage %remaining %emptytime" format_down = "No battery" status_chr = "󰂈 CHR" status_bat = "󱊢 BAT" status_unk = "? UNK" status_full = "󱊣 FULL" path = "/sys/class/power_supply/BAT%d/uevent" low_threshold = 10 last_full_capacity = true } volume master { format = "♪: %volume" format_muted = "♪: muted (%volume)" device = "default" mixer = "Master" mixer_idx = 0 } tztime madrid { format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" timezone = "Europe/Madrid" } memory { format = "%used/%total" threshold_degraded = "10%" format_degraded = "MEMORY: %free" } disk "/" { format = "%used/%total" } disk "/home" { format = "%used/%total" }
